sceneFacts.shortVersion: That "Pacheco Pass" sign? It was creative license for the film.
sceneFacts.longDescription: That "Pacheco Pass" sign? It was creative license for the film. The actual road shown was Quien Sabe Ranch Road in rural San Benito County.

sceneAnchor.sceneDescription:
[scene 7] 00:02:18–00:02:37
summary: The video clip shows a first-person view of a vehicle driving on a rural road with dry hills, accompanied by engine sounds and opening title text, creating an adventurous and energetic mood.
sceneAnchor.anchorElement: A highway sign for "Pacheco Pass" seen in the opening credits was a touch of "creative license"; the road shown was actually Quien Sabe Ranch Road in rural San Benito County.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Lou Diamond Phillips was older than his on-screen older brother.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Lou Diamond Phillips was older than his on-screen older brother. Phillips was 24 when cast as Ritchie, while Esai Morales was 23 when he scored the role of older half-brother Bob.

sceneAnchor.sceneDescription:
[scene 15] 00:04:57–00:05:18
summary: The clip shows a group of young adults interacting outdoors near a school building, with a focus on introductions and a conversation about joining a group, set in a casual, somewhat tense but friendly atmosphere.
cast on screen: Lou Diamond Phillips, Elizabeth Peña, Esai Morales
sceneAnchor.anchorElement: Lou Diamond Phillips, who played the younger Ritchie Valens, was actually a few months older than Esai Morales, who portrayed his older half-brother Bob, requiring Phillips to project youth.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: San Fernando High School was Ritchie Valens' real-life alma mater.
sceneFacts.longDescription: San Fernando High School was Ritchie Valens' real-life alma mater. Director Luis Valdez aimed to film at as many places where Valens and his family actually spent time.

sceneAnchor.sceneDescription:
[scene 39] 00:13:13–00:13:17
summary: The video shows the exterior of a high school building with a sign reading 'San Fernando High School' and a quiet street, while the subtitle indicates that a class is in session, suggesting a calm educational setting.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Bob Morales told the director to show his real-life struggles.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Bob Morales told the director to show his real-life struggles. He admitted to being "the bad guy" and blamed his drinking.

sceneAnchor.sceneDescription:
[scene 63] 00:20:59–00:21:28
summary: A tense and emotional confrontation between a woman and a shirtless man in a small, dimly lit room, where the woman reveals she is pregnant, leading to a charged atmosphere of frustration, loneliness, and conflict.
cast on screen: Elizabeth Peña, Esai Morales
sceneAnchor.anchorElement: During research, Ritchie's half-brother Bob Morales was remarkably candid about his struggles, openly admitting to being an alcoholic and abusive, and telling director Luis Valdez to include these truths.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Ritchie Valens' singing voice isn't Lou Diamond Phillips'.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Ritchie Valens' singing voice isn't Lou Diamond Phillips'. David Hidalgo of Los Lobos provided the vocals for all of Valens' songs in the film.

sceneAnchor.sceneDescription:
[scene 110] 00:36:18–00:36:35
summary: The video shows a band performing energetically on stage with a lead singer playing guitar, while a crowd of smiling and cheering people enjoy the lively atmosphere in an indoor venue.
cast on screen: Elizabeth Peña, Lou Diamond Phillips
sceneAnchor.anchorElement: While Lou Diamond Phillips convincingly portrayed Ritchie Valens' stage presence, the singing voice for all of Valens' songs in the film was actually performed by David Hidalgo of Los Lobos.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Ritchie's real-life romance with Donna was more casual than the film shows.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Ritchie's real-life romance with Donna was more casual than the film shows. His manager felt their relationship was "more akin to a casual acquaintance."

sceneAnchor.sceneDescription:
[scene 150] 00:49:37–00:49:54
summary: The video shows two men outdoors near a rabbit cage, with one man expressing a disturbing and aggressive attitude about sex, creating a tense and uncomfortable mood in a rural or backyard setting.
cast on screen: Lou Diamond Phillips
sceneAnchor.anchorElement: The film took artistic liberties with Ritchie's personal life; his real-life relationship with Donna was more casual, and he was not as innocent as depicted, having visited a bordello with his brother.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: That motorcycle belonged to the real Bob Morales.
sceneFacts.longDescription: That motorcycle belonged to the real Bob Morales. His 1974 Shovelhead made a cameo in the film.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Ritchie's fear of flying was real, from a tragic school accident.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Ritchie's fear of flying was real, from a tragic school accident. The film depicts his recurring nightmares about a mid-air collision over his junior high.

sceneAnchor.sceneDescription:
[scene 301] 01:40:16–01:40:37
summary: In a snowy nighttime setting, two men prepare a small plane for flight, with one man reassuring the other as they board the aircraft, creating a mood of cautious optimism and camaraderie.
sceneAnchor.anchorElement: Ritchie Valens' real-life fear of flying, depicted in the film, stemmed from a traumatic event where two planes collided over his school, killing three students.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: This is "the day the music died," immortalized by Don McLean.
sceneFacts.longDescription: This is "the day the music died," immortalized by Don McLean. Ritchie Valens died in a 1959 plane crash with Buddy Holly and The Big Bopper.

sceneAnchor.sceneDescription:
[scene 301] 01:40:16–01:40:37
summary: In a snowy nighttime setting, two men prepare a small plane for flight, with one man reassuring the other as they board the aircraft, creating a mood of cautious optimism and camaraderie.
sceneAnchor.anchorElement: The film includes a subtle nod to Don McLean's iconic song "American Pie," which famously refers to the plane crash that killed Valens, Buddy Holly, and The Big Bopper as "the day the music died."

sceneFacts.shortVersion: “La Bamba” by Los Lobos topped the charts for three weeks.
sceneFacts.longDescription: “La Bamba” by Los Lobos topped the charts for three weeks. Their rendition became a massive hit, surpassing Ritchie Valens' original.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: La Bamba challenged Hollywood's beliefs about Latino-focused films.
sceneFacts.longDescription: La Bamba challenged Hollywood's beliefs about Latino-focused films. Its success opened a "whole new revenue area" for studios.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Carlos Santana scored the film and won an award for it.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Carlos Santana scored the film and won an award for it. He and Miles Goodman received the 1988 BMI Film Music Award.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Lou Diamond Phillips beat out 500 actors to play Ritchie Valens.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Lou Diamond Phillips beat out 500 actors to play Ritchie Valens. Director Luis Valdez cast him for his "heart quality" despite some complaints about his heritage.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: La Bamba joined the National Film Registry in 2017.
sceneFacts.longDescription: La Bamba joined the National Film Registry in 2017. The Registry noted the film reinvigorated interest in Ritchie Valens' musical legacy.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: La Bamba made history with its simultaneous Spanish-language release.
sceneFacts.longDescription: La Bamba made history with its simultaneous Spanish-language release. It was Columbia Pictures' first major venture into the national Latino film market.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: With little info on Ritchie Valens, the script relied on family stories.
sceneFacts.longDescription: With little info on Ritchie Valens, the script relied on family stories. Director Luis Valdez interviewed his mother, brother, manager, and girlfriend for the screenplay.
